# Running Self-Hosted AI Agents

Customers are increasingly asking us the following question:

> How do I run AI agents on Oxide?

The initial answer is simple. You run AI agents the same way you run other workloads on Oxideââin virtual machines. Customers already run long-lived services in virtual machines, so running AI agents feels familiar.

However, AI agents arenât exactly long-lived servicesââthey fall somewhere between that and ephemeral CI/CD jobs, depending on how they are used. Run a long-lived agent that provisions sub-agents and it looks like the former. Run an agent to complete a bounded task using /goal and it looks like the latter.

Regardless of your use case, the workflow looks like this:

- Provision a virtual machine.

- Run the AI agent in the virtual machine.

- Clean up the virtual machine.

With that context, the more accurate answer is to run the AI agentâs orchestrator as a virtual machine, configured to create ephemeral virtual machines for each AI agent session. Iâll show how this works on our Oxide Cloud Computer using both Claude Code self-hosted environments and Amp self-hosted orbs.

## AI agents need CPUs

Before describing how to run AI agents on an Oxide Cloud Computer, itâs important to understand why AI agents need CPUs in the first place.

AI agents are just systems that perform inference and execute tool calls in a loop. Put another way, AI becomes "agentic" when GPU-based inference needs CPU-based tool execution.

The AI agent harness (e.g., Claude Code, Codex, Amp) is responsible for running this loop. The harness runs as a process on a CPU, communicating with an LLM over the network. When the LLM requests a tool call, the harness executes it on the CPU itâs running on and sends the result back to the LLM.

Without a CPU, you canât run the harness or execute tool calls.

AI agents need strong isolation for both security and performance. You donât want an AI agent to delete important data or duel with other AI agents and disrupt their execution.

Virtual machines provide stronger isolation than containers, making them well-suited for AI agents. This isolation comes at a cost, summarized by this table:

These questions are surprisingly difficult to work through, especially when documentation leaves out the details. Look at this quote from the Claude Code self-hosted environments documentation .

Not only does this push readers towards containers, and possibly worse isolation as a result, but it also has a tone of "just do the right thing" without telling readers how to do it. Excuse me, Claude, did you just tell me to go eff myself?

Needless to say, when our customers ask how to run AI agents on Oxide, they also ask how to do it specifically with virtual machines, not containers.

## AI agents on Oxide

Letâs see how to run AI agents on our Oxide Cloud Computer using virtual machines, specifically using Claude Code self-hosted environments and Amp self-hosted orbs . These were chosen due to their popularity in the industry and to showcase how different AI agents use certain Oxide features.

### Claude Code self-hosted environments

Claude Code self-hosted environments run Claude Code sessions on infrastructure you control, in this case the Oxide Cloud Computer. The orchestrator dynamically provisions ephemeral Oxide virtual machines to run Claude Code and deletes them when finished.

Hereâs the architecture:

The orchestrator virtual machine is the central component. Itâs a long-running virtual machine responsible for addressing the complexity mentioned in the previous section. Recall these questions:

For provisioning, the orchestrator virtual machine runs a claude command youâve likely never used:

claude self-hosted-runner orchestrator \ --environment-secret-file /etc/claude-self-hosted/environment-secret \ --hooks-dir /etc/claude-self-hosted/hooks \ --hook-concurrency 1 \ --hook-timeout 60 \ --expected-spawn-seconds 300

This command authenticates to the self-hosted environment using the --environment-secret-file option and waits for work orders, which are requests to create an ephemeral runner for a userâs Claude Code session. When there are no work orders, the number of ephemeral runners scales down to zero.

The --hooks-dir option is, to borrow an LLM-ism, "load-bearing." It points to a directory containing hooks the orchestrator will call when work orders come in. The only hook available is spawn-runner , which, when called, must create the ephemeral virtual machine running the AI agent process. The AI agent process is another claude command youâve likely never used:

claude self-hosted-runner \ --capacity 1 \ --base-dir /var/lib/claude-self-hosted \ --use-anthropic-git-proxy \ --configure-git

The --capacity 1 option ensures the process only runs a single Claude Code session to support our ephemeral architecture, while the --use-anthropic-git-proxy and --configure-git options ensure that your connected Git repositories can be safely cloned within the virtual machine.

To make cleanup easier, the ephemeral virtual machine is configured to power off once the AI agent process has finished. There are a few ways to do this, but a popular way is to create a systemd service that runs at startup. The service then runs the AI agent process and runs poweroff after it exits.

A stopped virtual machine is the signal used for cleanup. Unfortunately, the orchestrator does not have a cleanup-runner hook, so the burden of cleanup is on us. I chose to run a separate reaper process that periodically polls the Oxide API for stopped virtual machines matching the desired name prefix. When it finds a matching virtual machine, it deletes it and its boot disk, freeing up resources for more Claude Code sessions.

If everything is wired up correctly, youâll be able to select your self-hosted environment when you create a Claude Code session on https://claude.ai . You could also run claude with the --environment option, though youâll need to ask your Claude administrator for the self-hosted environment ID to pass as its argument.

If you want to try this yourself, Iâve put together a showcase describing how to use Claude Code self-hosted environments with Oxide. Find the code at oxidecomputer/showcase .

### Amp self-hosted orbs

Amp self-hosted orbs run Amp threads on infrastructure you control, in this case the Oxide Cloud Computer. The provider dynamically provisions ephemeral Oxide virtual machines to run Amp orbs and deletes them when finished.

The Amp orb provider runs an amp command that authenticates to Amp and waits for requests to spawn, pause, and delete Amp orbs:

AMP_ORB_PROVIDER_TOKEN = 'aop_live...' amp orb provider dispatch.sh

The dispatch.sh script can contain any logic you wish, as long as it adheres to the dispatch contract defined by Amp, which is really just responding to the ORB_OPERATION values spawn , pause , and delete . Hereâs a pseudocode version of the dispatch script I used:

remove_instance () { oxide instance stop --project " $PROJECT " --instance " $orb_name " oxide instance delete --project " $PROJECT " --instance " $orb_name " } case " $ORB_OPERATION " in spawn ) remove_instance if oxide disk view --project " $PROJECT " --disk " $orb_name " ; then boot_disk = $( attach_disk " $orb_name " ) # resume from orb's disk else boot_disk = $( new_disk " $orb_name " " $ORB_IMAGE " ) # new orb from the image fi # User data starts `amp orb bootstrap` as `user` with this spawn's ORB_TOKEN. oxide instance create --project " $PROJECT " \ --json-body <( instance_body " $boot_disk " " $ORB_TOKEN ") ;; pause ) remove_instance # the disk is kept ;; delete ) remove_instance oxide disk delete --project " $PROJECT " --disk " $orb_name " ;; esac

Ampâs pause and delete operations free us from relying on a stopped virtual machine as the signal for cleanup. Instead, we can delete the instance but keep its boot disk for pause and delete the instance and its boot disk for delete . This significantly simplifies the overall architecture and deployment compared to Claude Code self-hosted environments.

If everything is wired up correctly, youâll be able to select your self-hosted orb provider when you create an Amp thread on https://ampcode.com . You could also run amp with the --orb-provider option, using the provider name as the argument.

If you want to try this yourself, Iâve put together a showcase describing how to use Amp self-hosted orbs with Oxide. Find the code at oxidecomputer/showcase .

## Tomorrowâs AI agents

Our Oxide Cloud Computer has the right primitives for todayâs AI agentsââvirtual machines with strong isolation, disks with solid performance, control over VPC networking, and an elastic API to dynamically provision everything. Even so, weâre looking ahead to meet the needs of tomorrowâs AI agents.

Conversations with current and prospective customers about AI agents have centered around the following themes:

- Security

- Scale

- Cold-start latency

- Cleanup

Security is where most conversations start, especially as the number of reported CVEs increases across the industry. Weâve already discussed the strong isolation provided by virtual machines, but our security story doesnât stop there. Our Oxide Cloud Computer has silos for tenancy and resource quota enforcement, projects for network isolation, and VPC firewall rules to block undesirable network traffic. Additionally, our removal of the BIOS, along with the virtual machine attestation work discussed in RFD 605 , provides a secure foundation for AI agent workloads.

If you run many AI agents, you may be wondering about scale. You can create as many virtual machines as you can fit on your Oxide Cloud Computer, but weâre working on multi-rack capabilities to expand a siloâs capacity beyond a single rack. Once released, this will simplify the management of AI agents across multiple racks.

Our API makes virtual machine provisioning trivial from an operational standpoint, but it can take tens of seconds or even minutes after an API request before a virtual machine is scheduled, booted, and running a workload. This affects users in the form of cold-start latency, which a warm pool can help mitigate, but not entirely eliminate. We accepted the latency in this blog post, but our goal is to reduce it as much as possible.

Cleaning up virtual machines is also trivial using the Oxide API, but, depending on the AI agent, there isnât always a simple way to know when the workload has finished. In this blog post, we handled this by treating a stopped virtual machine as the signal that the workload has finished. This required us to wrap our AI agent process in a systemd service that runs poweroff after the AI agent process exits, along with a reaper process to poll the Oxide API for virtual machines to clean up. Not the best user experience, especially if the AI agent architecture doesnât provide a delete operation, but weâre exploring how to make this experience behave like a container that exits when the main process is finished.

Iâve made it this far without talking about microVMs, but the microVM primitive is exactly what some infrastructure providers are using to improve the user experience of running AI agents without sacrificing the strong isolation theyâve come to rely on from virtual machines.
